title: Cabbage Patch Kids: Must-Have Toy of the Century
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Cabbage Patch Kids doll craze, from Xavier Roberts' Little People and Babyland General Hospital in Cleveland, Georgia, through the Coleco partnership, the 1983 shortages and chaos, the later license owners and relaunches, and the disputed origin story involving folk artist Martha Nelson Thomas and her "little doll babies," with a lawsuit that was settled. They also cover the Garbage Pail Kids parody and close with a listener email about beavers damming doorways.
topics: Milwaukee DJ prank Cabbage Patch Kids

segments.title: Opening banter and personal Cabbage Patch Kid stories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic as the third time the show has covered Cabbage Patch Kids and trade stories about their childhood dolls and the value of vintage Little People dolls.

segments.title: What Cabbage Patch Kids were and the Christmas craze
segments.summary: The hosts describe the doll as a must-have Christmas toy of the era, its unusual look, a journal article describing it, and a rumor that Ronald Reagan had the design managed to acclimate Americans to mutant offspring.

segments.title: The enchanted origin story versus the real story
segments.summary: Josh recounts the fanciful origin story on the official website, with a bunny bee, a waterfall tunnel, and a cabbage patch. He then gives the official account: Xavier Roberts at Truett-McConnell College learned German needle molding and began making baby dolls in 1977.

segments.title: Little People dolls and Original Appalachian Artworks
segments.summary: Roberts sold handmade Little People as adoptable dolls with birth certificates for about forty dollars, at craft fairs and at Unicoi State Park. He founded Original Appalachian Artworks, which opened Babyland General in Cleveland, Georgia, where staff dressed as medical workers staged births of the dolls.

segments.title: Partnership with Coleco and mass production changes
segments.summary: Demand outran Roberts' supply, so he partnered with Coleco in 1982. Coleco renamed the dolls Cabbage Patch Kids, replaced the handmade cloth heads with machine-made vinyl heads, shrank them to about sixteen inches, added variety in ethnicity, skin tone, and features, and set adoption fees near thirty dollars.
topics: name change to Cabbage Patch Kids

segments.title: Shortages, riots, and the 1983 Christmas frenzy
segments.summary: Coleco sold over three million dolls by the end of 1983 but could not keep up with demand. Stores saw fights and crowds; a Zayre manager in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania tossed dolls into a crowd. A Milwaukee DJ prank had people show up at the Brewers stadium to catch dolls dropped from a plane. The hosts discuss whether the scarcity was intentional and the resulting secondary market.

segments.title: Sales peak, pop culture, and later relaunches
segments.summary: Sales reached about two billion dollars in 1984. The dolls appeared in pop culture, including a Christopher Xavier doll on a Space Shuttle mission and as an Olympic mascot in Barcelona. Coleco went bankrupt, and the license passed to Mattel, Toys R Us, and then Play Along. Failed attempts such as talking dolls, a swimming doll, and the Snack Time doll are discussed, along with a relaunch with cloth bodies.

segments.title: Martha Nelson Thomas and the origin dispute
segments.summary: The hosts describe how folk artist Martha Nelson Thomas made similar needle-molded little doll babies in the 1970s. Roberts initially sold her dolls, then marked them up and went on to make his own after a dispute. Thomas sued, and after years of litigation Roberts settled for an undisclosed sum. The hosts note that Roberts signed each doll's butt, which made copyright hard to claim for Thomas's unsigned dolls.

segments.title: Garbage Pail Kids parody
segments.summary: Topps' Garbage Pail Kids parodied Cabbage Patch Kids with deformed, diseased characters. Roberts objected, and the parody was changed enough to avoid looking officially tied to Cabbage Patch Kids. Art Spiegelman was an art director on the series.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Hosts note the stat of 130 million dolls born over thirty-two years and move to a break.

segments.title: Listener mail about beavers
segments.summary: A listener from Spain writes about the beaver Beav, a beaver raised after being abandoned that drags objects to dam a doorway. The hosts read the email and thank the listener, Carrie Keeley.
